stem: Why do physical accessibility standards favor lever-style door handles over traditional round knobs?

options.text: They can be gripped from above, so users with limited hand strength can pull the door open.
options.rationale: Lever handles are operated by pressing down, not by gripping from above and pulling.

options.text: They stay engaged after being pressed, so users do not need to hold the handle while the door opens.
options.rationale: A lever returns to its resting position after the latch releases; the door is opened by pushing or pulling the door itself.

options.text: They cost less to install and maintain, so accessible hardware fits within limited public budgets.
options.rationale: Accessibility standards set minimum requirements for usability, not for the installation or maintenance cost of hardware.

options.text: They can be operated with a fist or elbow, which keeps the wrist in a neutral position.
options.rationale: Levers can be depressed with an arm, elbow, or closed fist, so they do not require the tight grasp and wrist twist a round knob demands.

explanation: Round door knobs require tight grasping, pinching, and wrist twisting, which presents a significant barrier to people with arthritis, missing limbs, or neurological conditions. Lever handles can be operated without fine motor control using a downward press of a fist or elbow.

references.title: IAAP CPACC Body of Knowledge v4.0
